section_title: How do we help one another keep going?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 12 Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees. 13 Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed. 14 Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.

15 See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many. 16 See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright. 17 For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.

context_lines: The response to discipline includes renewed strength and care for those struggling. The writer draws on [Isaiah 35:3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/35.htm) and the straight-path picture in [Proverbs 4:26–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/proverbs/4.htm). The aim is healing and a steady course, rather than allowing weakness to become a departure from the way.
Peace and holiness are to be pursued together. Care for people does not mean treating destructive conduct as harmless, and pursuing holiness does not make peace with others unimportant.

The warning about a root of bitterness recalls [Deuteronomy 29:18–19](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/29.htm), where a person turns toward other gods while imagining that stubborn disobedience will still bring peace. The concern is a corrupting influence that can spread through the community, beyond the ordinary hurt feelings the English word bitterness may suggest.

Esau supplies the example of treating something valuable as expendable for an immediate appetite. [Genesis 25:29–34](https://biblehub.com/bsb/genesis/25.htm) records the birthright bargain, and [27:34–38](https://biblehub.com/bsb/genesis/27.htm) his later tears over the blessing. The warning urges care now, before a careless choice brings consequences that cannot simply be undone.
common_interpretation_lines: [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/hebrews/12.htm) and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-epistle-to-the-hebrews/) understand the strengthening and watchfulness as responsibilities that involve the community, rather than permission to abandon those who struggle. They take the pursuit of holiness seriously.

They place different emphases on Esau’s tears. Wesley says no change could regain the lost blessing. Calvin distinguishes sorrow over loss from a sincere return to God, and explicitly says God welcomes the repentant sinner. He does not read Esau as proof that genuine repentance is always refused.

The [USCCB note](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/hebrews/12) connects Esau with the warning about repentance after falling away. That is a commentary reading; the [Catholic Catechism, 1446](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_two/article_4/vi_the_sacrament_of_penance_and_reconciliation.index.html), also teaches reconciliation for serious sin after baptism. Neither the wording here nor that note should be made into a claim that every failure leaves someone unable to seek God.
god_plan_lines: [Ephesians 5:25–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/5.htm) describes Christ loving the church and giving Himself to cleanse it and present it holy. The holiness pursued here belongs within His purpose for the people He loves.

[1 Corinthians 12:25–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/12.htm) describes members of one body sharing care, suffering and joy. Strengthening a weakened person serves that common life, rather than treating the Christian journey as a private contest against everyone else.
